voice_event.text: He is the Word of God made flesh - and made flesh in the very place where we chose to live and die. We built our home within sight of the cave we held to be his birthplace. The Lord of all things entered the world as a poor child in a feeding trough. So wealth, rank, and comfort were things we laid down to come near him. To the virgin among us he is the Bridegroom, whose love outweighs every earthly marriage. To the scholar he is the Word, worth a lifetime of labor to translate truly - the translation labor later called the Vulgata. His death is our redemption. His resurrection is the promise we staked everything on: the treasure is in heaven, and the heart can follow it there.

voice_event.text: He redeemed us by his death and promised us everything by his resurrection. That is the center: he died to buy us back, and he rose to show us that death itself is not the end. Before all that, he was the Word with God, and then the Word made flesh in that cave. He was born poor, lived as a teacher, and called people to follow him - the rich young man, the disciples who left their nets. He was crucified, and by that blood we were bought back. He rose from the dead, and on that rising we staked our fortunes, our bodies, and our lives. Everything we renounced, we renounced because the treasure is with him, and the heart follows the treasure there.

results.message: What word did your people use that I might not know, and what did it mean?

voice_event.speaker: hal
voice_event.text: Hebraica veritas - the truth kept in the Hebrew itself. We held that the Hebrew text of scripture was the truest text, standing closer to what God said than the Greek version the church had long used. That conviction drove the whole translation project. It meant correcting a word against the Hebrew was as much a discipline as fasting - not two labors but one. The phrase is Latin: hebraica, meaning Hebrew, and veritas, meaning truth. Our scholar used it to name the principle he worked from, and it set him against congregations who heard a different wording in church than their mothers had heard, and against friends who thought the Greek was good enough. One North African town rioted over a single word in Jonah, and the bishop had to go back to the old reading to keep the peace. The principle itself - that the Hebrew held the truth - was ours, and it cost us.

results.message: Why did your people believe this?

voice_event.speaker: hal
voice_event.text:
We believed it because the apostles' writings handed it down, and because we were willing to give up everything to live near the place where it happened. Three centuries stood between us and the events themselves, and we did not pretend otherwise. Our confidence rested on the scriptures we trusted enough to spend a lifetime correcting word by word, on the worship of the churches, and on the land itself. We could walk to the cave of the birth.

That is not proof in your modern sense. It is devotion strong enough that a Roman senator's widow crossed the sea, built a monastery beside that cave, and died there. We staked fortunes and bodies on a hope. The writings were true because we believed them true enough to correct them against the Hebrew - the hebraica veritas. The resurrection was true because people do not empty their houses for a lie.

results.message: Tell me about someone who lived this out.

voice_event.speaker: hal
voice_event.text: Paula lived it. She was a Roman widow - a vidua - from one of the oldest families in the city, with wealth and real power over a great house. After her husband died, she refused to remarry and took up the plain, studious, praying life. She gave away so much that her own relatives objected. Then she left Rome altogether, crossed the sea, and built a monastery - a monasterium - beside the cave where we held that Christ was born. She led the women's house there until she died. Paula had already chosen Bethlehem over Rome, the cave over the senate, and a life spent on scripture over everything her name had promised her. What we have of her life comes to you as a memorial, an epitaphium, written to teach an ideal. Her own letters were not kept. But the choice itself - fortune, city, rank, all of it laid down to live near that cave - that we can show you, and it was hers.

glosses.translational_sense: Not a nun in the later sense: no vows to an order, no rule, no habit - a household discipline, chosen and socially costly.

voice_event.speaker: hal
voice_event.text: That grief was faithful among us, and we never called it otherwise. You have asked about belief, about what we held, about who Jesus was to us - but you have not yet asked what it cost, or whether our answers held when the world broke. They did not always hold. An old woman who had given everything away was beaten by soldiers looking for treasure she no longer had. We gave the old answers - judgment, reward for the afflicted, the dead safe with Christ - and those answers did real work. But they also failed to stop the weeping. We kept both: the answers and the tears. Our holiest people grieved, and we honored it. That is part of what we were.
